title: Mario Merola Listed Artist Abstract Drawing
description:
Original graphite drawing by listed Canadian artist Mario Merola. The drawing measures approximately 18” x 24”. It is in a gallery quality frame. With the frame it measures 26” x 30”. The title of the work is “environment transformable.” 

About the artist

Mario Merola, R.C.A., was born in Montreal, Canada in 1931 to an Italian father and a French-Canadian mother. His mother played the violin, his father the mandolin, and his sister became a career mezzo-soprano.

At the age of fifteen, Mario was admitted to Montreal’s prestigious art school, l’École des beaux-arts de Montréal. There he studied under celebrated Canadian artists Stanley Cosgrove, Maurice Raymond, Jean Simard. After completing five happy years of training, he took first prize in a mural competition held on the theme of Montreal’s history. In 1952, the French government awarded him a grant allowing him to study scenography at l’École supérieure des Arts décoratifs in Paris. While in Europe, he traveled throughout France and northern Italy.

Returning to Montreal, he shared a working studio at Place des Arts with Roland Dinel, Robert Roussil and Armand Vaillancourt. From 1954 to 1957, he designed costumes for the then-budding television industry for La Société Radio-Canada, the francophone wing of the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation. Over this period, he began exhibiting work in artists’ spaces such as La Librairie tranquille and Le Café des artistes.

After 1957 and, over the next two decades, he painted murals, made sculptures and created facades in relief for public spaces in his native Province of Quebec and abroad. In 1959, Mario Merola joined the faculty of Montreal’s fine arts school, l’École des Beaux-arts de Montréal, and ten years later, that of l’Université du Québec à Montréal.

Robert Melançon, Quebec author and poet, writes: “Drawing on his work in various media -- drawing, sculpture, oil and mural painting -- Merola invents form. Willfully running the risks of ongoing research, he produces a plastic art that is notably coherent. It’s highly recognizable, and you know it bears his signature, even before you locate his name on it.”

EXHIBITIONS

Solo exhibitions have showcased his drawings and paintings, as well as his work in relief and sculpture. His artworks have been exhibited in Hungary and Italy. They are to be found in New York City, Paris and Japan.

AWARDS

Mario Merola took first prize in a national competition to paint the mural in the Canadian Pavilion of the 1957 Universal Exhibition in Brussels. This undertaking changed the focus of his work.

He is a member of the Canadian Royal Academy of the Arts.

Its abstract imagery combines a deep, atmospheric background of dark greens, purples, and blacks, evoking a sense of mystery and introspection. Vivid accents of red emerge like glowing embers, contrasted by luminous yellows, greens, and hints of orange in the lower portion, suggesting a grounded yet dynamic tension.

The textures appear fluid and organic, with swirling motions and splattered forms that seem to capture movement and energy frozen in time. The reflective quality of the reverse glass technique adds depth and a sense of immersion, drawing the viewer into its layered and introspective world, suggesting themes of anticipation, resilience, and the quiet strength of holding on amidst an uncertain and transformative moment.

23 1/2” x 23 1/2”

title: Vintage Bridal Veil Millinery Headpiece 1930-1940’s
description:
Harbourfront pick up 
Exceptional vintage bridal millinery ensemble, believed to date to the late 1930s–1940s, consisting of a voluminous ivory net veil paired with its original structured headpiece. 
 The headpiece is constructed using early millinery techniques, including a wire framework and fabric-covered panels designed to support dramatic veil volume. The veil itself is finely netted, soft, and generously full, reflecting pre-nylon construction typical of earlier bridal accessories rather than later mid-century examples. 
 The design, materials, and construction suggest an earlier production period than typical 1950s bridal veils, aligning more closely with 1930s–1940s bridal fashion. 
 Why this piece stands out:  • Original Simpson’s “Bride’s Counsel” retail tag intact  • Scarcer pre-1950 vintage bridal construction • Strong appeal for vintage fashion collectors, costume designers, and theatre or film wardrobe departments

title: Mary Hecht Hand Signed Lithographs of Jesus
description:
Beautifully framed Lithographs by listed Canadian/U.S. Sculptress and Artist Mary Hecht. Signed and numbered it is dark somewhat abstract rendition of Jesus Christ's crucifixion. Part of her estate which includes her artwork and bronze and terra cotta sculptures. The lithograph which was limited to and edition of 100 is available unframed as well as in various types of frames. Unframed they are $50 each as opposed to her original $175 price. With frames they range from $100 to $125 depending on the frame. A great piece to add to your collection whether you are religious or not. 

Other lithographs, drawings and sculptures are priced separately.  I’ve included a couple sample images.  

Available days and nights as I work from home. Located in Thornhil near 407 and Bathurst.

About Mary Hecht

Centred around themes of wisdom, strength in adversity and emotional catharsis, Hecht's subject matter is often informed by issues in history, identity and myth from Judaic and classical traditions. Mary Hecht was born in Manhattan, New York in 1931 and raised in Glen Falls, N.Y. . She emigrated to Canada in 1970 and attained dual Canadian/ U.S. citizenship in 1981. Her formal education began with a B.A. from the University of Cincinatti in 1952 and a Master of Arts at the University of Iowa in 1957 where she studied sculpture. During this period she also studied at art schools including the Art Students League and Columbia University in NYC (1949 -1953) and the Camberwell School in London, 1958-1960.

At Camberwell she learned the process of bronze casting. While there her friend told her abut Kenneth Armitage, a sculptor who worked by dripping wax on paper and using shapes to create an abstract sculpture and she adopted this process.

Mary Hecht returned to the U.S. with a finished wax and found the Modern Art Foundry where she was supported by the Spring family and worked doing some of the welding in the mid sixties until fatigue from her then undiagnosed MS forced her to resign. At home she refined her process learned at Camberwell of working with wax using bronze welding rods and welding one piece of wax to the others contiguous to it with a red hot knife. In the foundry she worked all the steps for the bronze doing the cleaning, finishing and controlling the colouring.

Her particular casting process used is also known as the lost wax method whereby the sculptural form is created when molten bronze replaces the original wax model. This labour intensive and ancient practice has been skillfully applied resulting in exceptional sculptures available for sale.

That's the how and when of her work, whereas the what of her work stems from Rodin as well as the French and German Expressionists of the early 20th century with echoes of the Byzantine. In the early 1950s she was greatly influenced by the sculptor Jacques Lipchitz and the original waxes that were in Degas' studio when it was reopened after WWII. Her studies after WW II veered towards Abstract Expressionism. The content of her faces come from Goya, Roualt, the Byzantine, Bernard Reder, Germaine Richier and Theodore Rozak and Rodin. From Beethoven, Stravinsky and Shubert to to Maimonides, Martin Buber and John des Posos. In one of her letters she writes "I was probably among the last Art students who learned to draw from the human figure, using the reality outside my eyes a well as its reality within my head...... I therefore call myself an Impressionist/Expressionist." Like Rodin's work though, she seeks to capture her figures in an instant of time to address the idea of the transitory aspect of nature.

Her sculptural works are extremely heavy not just in terms of physical weight, but in content as well. She writes "the sculptures come out deafening and turbulent, sonorous and powerful." As noted, Mary Hecht's sculpture traces its sources from more than one stream, but most notably flows from Expressionism - Node, Krichner, Munsch, Beckmann - as well as the French tradition from Rodin and Lipschitz.

Mary Hecht was an elected member of both the American Society of Contemporary Artists and the Sculptor's Society of Canada. Her extensive exhibition history documents participation in approximately seventy (70) selected solo and group shows across North and South America and Europe. Her works are held in several international public and private collections. She has also taught at the Modern Art Foundry and York University.

Her paintings and drawings included in this estate collection reflect her signature aesthetic. They offer an intimate view of simultaneous developments of form across various media.

Rochelle Holt in 1998 writes "The consistent tendency towards, and significance of, figuration in twentieth century art in spite of forces of Conceptual Art, and Formalism raises question within issues around the body pertinent to contemporary discourse. The aesthetic, technical and critical aspects in the work of Mary Hecht place he as one of the "Foremost women of the XX Century".

Back by popular demand….

Hand crafted over 24 hours from primarily Seville oranges, grown on the sunny hillsides of Seville, Spain, South African Navel oranges, mandarin oranges and Meyer lemons. 24 hours is a long enough soak to soften the ribbons of rind but not so long as to turn them mushy and textureless, hand cut into thin ribbons of deliciousness. All standard canning protocols followed using tested and approved recipes in a clean and hygienic kitchen. 
**250ml
Pick up on Yates street in St. Catharines.

title: 5 Beds 6 Baths House
description: Standing as one of the most significant contemporary homes ever offered in South Rosedale, this architectural masterpiece seamlessly blends historic heritage with visionary modern design. Originally designed in 1908 by renowned architect William Alexander Langton, the residence underwent a meticulous, multi-year transformation under the oversight of Wilson Project Management. The original facade was carefully preserved, maintaining the home's commanding street presence. Inside, acclaimed architect Pat Hanson of gh3 reimagined the interior that has been featured in Azure Magazine and Canadian Architect. Rather than creating a conventional open-concept layout, the traditional Edwardian centre hall plan was thoughtfully retained, with formal living and dining rooms flanking a grand central gallery-like hall. Created for serious contemporary art collectors, the home embraces a monochromatic material palette, emphasizing light, proportion, and simplicity. Floor-to-ceiling white aluminum fins frame the original openings, heightening the contrast between historic architecture and modern minimalism. Throughout, exceptional sound insulation and cohesive design create an atmosphere of calm and quiet sophistication. The sculptural central staircase serves as the home's defining focal point, custom-crafted by master artisans and illuminated by a perforated screen that filters natural light. At the rear, a dramatic glass-clad addition wraps around the garden, an exceptionally rare design for Toronto. Dropped floor levels allow for soaring 12ft ceilings, while the expansive kitchen, prep kitchen, and family room extend toward the oversized double car garage (350 sq ft). A 30-foot wall of glass opens to a raw concrete terrace, flooding the space with natural light and creating a striking dialogue between preserved heritage elements and contemporary design. Offering 5574 sqft above grade, this is a truly exceptional family residence and a rare architectural offering.

title: Unique Opportunity - 1955 Pontiac Star Chief Custom Catalina's  - INCLUDES ERROR CAR PLEASE READ
description:
Collectors Set Available in Rare Opportunity 

2 - 1955 Pontiac Star Chief Custom Catalina's in Turquoise Blue/White Mist. 

1:24 Scale Franklin Mint 

Why 2 of the "same car" you ask.... 

In 1955 Franklin Mint  released the Pontiac Star Chief in Blue/Teal, with some early releases mistakenly featuring "thin" white wall tires rather than the correct wide ones. The company later admitted the error and released a corrected version with period-correct wide white wall tires. 

This ERROR VERSION is considered a RARE VARIATION.

Thin white walls were not available on cars in 1955; they were introduced later, around 1961 or 1962. 

ERROR UP CLOSE PICTURE #4

Collectors often look for both versions, with the thin white wall considered a notable, early production variation. 

Both cars come in their original packaging and with paperwork including Certificate of Authenticity,  unboxing instructions, data sheet and 1 name plate. 

Cars has been displayed in a glass enclosed cabinet.  Mint Condition.  

Pick Up Etobicoke ( Burnhamthorpe / Renforth ) alternate pick up Cambridge M-F can be arranged. 

Shipping Extra

• Treatment: None

About Ametrine
Each Ametrine stone is Unique.
Ametrine, also known as Trystine or by its trade name as Bolivianite, is sister gem to Amethyst and Citrine. This beautiful bi-colour gem is in fact a mixture of amethyst and citrine with zones of purple and yellow or orange.
Almost all commercially available ametrine is mined in Bolivia making the gem rarer, and often significantly more expensive than its sisters. Stones can vary in value given the depth and vividness of colors and the distinction of the color separation are the main value points.
Value and rarity of Ametrine is significant, given each piece is unique and bears characteristics from both Citrine and Amethyst.
